title: MEMENTO: Teaching LLMs to Manage Their Own Context
clean_title: MEMENTO: Teaching LLMs to Manage Their Own Context
summary: Reasoning models think in long, unstructured streams with no mechanism for compressing or organizing their own intermediate state. We introduce MEMENTO: a method that teaches models to segment reasoning into blocks, compress each block into a meme...
clean_summary:
Reasoning models often process information in long, unstructured streams without the ability to compress or organize their intermediate states. MEMENTO is introduced as a method that teaches models to segment their reasoning into manageable blocks and compress each block into a meme-like representation.

This approach enables more efficient reasoning by allowing models to maintain context and manage information better. The method aims to enhance the performance of large language models by improving their ability to handle complex reasoning tasks.

title: Open-World Evaluations for Measuring Frontier AI Capabilities
clean_title: Open-World Evaluations for Measuring Frontier AI Capabilities
summary: Benchmark-based evaluation remains important for tracking frontier AI progress. But it can both overstate and understate deployed capability because it privileges tasks that can be precisely specified, automatically graded, easy to optimize for, a...
clean_summary: Benchmark-based evaluation remains important for tracking frontier AI progress. However, it can both overstate and understate deployed capability because it favors tasks that can be precisely specified, automatically graded, and easy to optimize for, while potentially missing broader or more complex abilities. The work discusses the need for open-world evaluation methods that better reflect real-world deployment scenarios and capabilities.

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
a lot of people have been talking about o3/r1 confabulating things like "checking the docs" or "using a laptop to verify a computation" as an example of reasoning model's misalignment. however, while it may be misleading to some users, i don't think it's an example of models lying for the sake of lying. rather, i think phrases like "let me check the docs" are discovered by RL in much the same way as "hmm..." or "wait but," because they promote accurate recall--when someone uses them in pretraining, they generally precede an accurate statement about the documentation in question!
here's a quick test (see caveats below) I ran by prefilling two different thinking traces on r1. i asked r1 a question about QGIS and it confabulated looking up something about the C++ api. when i replaced that confabulation with a straightforward statement prefix, the recalled constructor signature was more likely to use a dissimilar variable name and a different pointer syntax convention from the documentation!
that's to say, i think reasoning models confabulate taking actions in the real world because when they do, the resulting continuations are more similar to the real world, and thus more likely to be useful for an accurate answer. this is a well-known technique among people who work with base models, so it's not that surprising that RL also discovers it.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GqEfNtqbAAAzA13.png

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Awesome stuff. Can’t wait for the write up
Quoting @gharik
Because we started from quiet star we had developed and have been using a slightly different version of grpo. We believe it may be a lower variance gradient and therefore possibly increase stability. We will write this up later but wanted to share it now so other people can use the idea.
For each problem, we produce N1 chain of thoughts but then after that for each chain of thought we produce N2 answers, which for some domains is pretty cheap because answers are much shorter. Then we compute an advantage per answer for each thought and we normalize inside the answer group, and use that to reinforce the answerer. Then following that we produce a cot advantage per thought within a problem and use that to reinforce the thought.
The increase in the number of answers gets better, as in lower variance, advantages for both the answers as well as the thoughts.

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
"RL with only one training example" and "Test-Time RL" are two recent papers that I found fascinating.
In the "One Training example" paper
the authors find one question and ask the model to solve it again and again. Every time, the model tries 8 times (the Group in GRPO), and a gradient step is performed, to increase the reward which is a very simple verification of the correct answers, repeated thousands of times on the same problem.
The shocking finding is that the model does not overfit to this one question: RL on one example, makes the model better in MATH500 and other benchmarks.
(If instead you did SFT repeating one training question-solution finetuning, the model would quickly memorize this answer and overfit). But with RL, the model has to solve the problem itself, since it only sees the question, not the answer. Every time it produces different answers, and this seems to prevent overfitting. The other papers are relying on the same phenomenon: you can have a small number of training questions and re-solve them thousands of times. You can do this for the test set (as test-time RL does) and still not overfit. We also independently saw this by doing RL training on half the test set and seeing benefits in the other half for BFCL agents.
My thought now is that this shows our RL learning algorithm must be extremely inefficient. When a human is learning by solving a math puzzle, they immediately learn what they can learn by solving it once (or twice). No further benefit would come by assigning the same homework problem to students a tenth time. But in RL, we keep asking the model to re-solve the same question thousands of times, and the model slowly gets better. We should be able to have much better RL learning algorithms since the information is there. (1/2)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gqn-aESaMAAMfOy.jpg

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Informal Soft-Token Theorem (obvious, proof omitted):
Iterative tasks that require D-dimensional states force hard-token decoders (e.g., ordinary LLMs) into a Θ(D) per-iteration generation bottleneck. Allowing soft-token generations removes this bottleneck, expanding the set of expressible functions by Ω(embed_dim) and shrinking test-time compute to O(D/embed_dim).
..whether such models are trainable is another question!

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Why I'm Too Tired to Try Your New Model
... but I still will for now
Testing new models is exhausting. Public benchmarks don't capture how well a model will perform for YOUR use case. Unlike 2023, to measure the difference across models, you have to invest serious hours experimenting to get signal on whether the are meaningful improvements for the tasks you actually care about.
And even when you do find a "better" model, there's huge friction in switching. Migrating apps/apis has to break through massive inertia. What if your current model provider offers a better model next week, is it worth the switch?
So my expectation is that, unless there are new use cases that significantly disrupt things, the model provider landscape will remain surprisingly stable, with most people defaulting to what they already use.
Model providers can't rely on marginal performance gains on GPQA, or even fancy demos to win market share anymore. Maybe new, crazy cool products?
I don't know, I'm not an expert, but hill climbing on benchmarks and demoing rotating 4D cubes with spinning spheres inside them, each engraved with Fermat's last theorem in all languages and written in reverse (as mind blowing as it sounds) won't win users. You'll need something genuinely disruptive.

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Great to see the additive dataset methodology we proposed in Phi-4-reasoning adopted in open-r1.
Tldr: optimize data mixture per reasoning domain, and combine in final run for generalized performance. This is a game changer for reducing data ablation costs.
Quoting @_lewtun
Happy to share 💭 Mixture of Thoughts 💭
A curated, general reasoning dataset that trims down over 1M samples from public datasets to ~350k through an extensive set of ablations 🧑‍🍳
Models trained on this mix match or exceed the performance of DeepSeek's distilled models -- not just on math/code but also on scientific benchmarks like GPQA
We also validate that the "additive" methodology from Phi-4-reasoning really works! You can optimise the data mixture independently per reasoning domain and then bring it all together for the final run 🔥
Link to the dataset ⤵️
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gr414sbWAAA7hdV.jpg

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Random labels helping makes sense when P(correct|random)>0 since the x-change rate of accuracy is much higher for true positive rather than false negative/false positive examples.
Wrong labels working makes little sense, and is a result of undertraining + trajectories being close to correct still allows you to learn, as in the long term it should converge to wrong trajectories.
Quoting @StellaLisy
🤯 We cracked RLVR with... Random Rewards?!
Training Qwen2.5-Math-7B with our Spurious Rewards improved MATH-500 by:
- Random rewards: +21%
- Incorrect rewards: +25%
- (FYI) Ground-truth rewards: + 28.8%

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
every paper that does "something"+"RL" and it's only on Qwen2.5, should seriously state that on the title.
Quoting @zihaozhou_
Recently, I saw the papers "rl on one sample" and "spurious reward". The findings are interesting, but they are indeed expected. In fact, the math solving ability of the Qwen models is really easy to activate—𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 !🤣
I'd like to share some interesting observations we made in March: 𝐁𝐲 𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚 𝐬𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐭 𝐰𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐡 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐯𝐲 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐭, 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥 𝐚𝐥𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐲 𝐞𝐱𝐡𝐢𝐛𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐠 𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐡 𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐢𝐧 𝐚 𝐳𝐞𝐫𝐨-𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐭 𝐬𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 , 𝐬𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐑𝐋.
As shown in Figure 1, we use the Mathstral prompt (just "please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \\boxed{}") to 4 Qwen base models and achieve very strong performance. 𝐎𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟏.𝟓𝐁 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝟑𝐁 𝐦𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥𝐬, 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐮𝐥𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧 𝐛𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐢𝐫 𝐑𝐋-𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 (the recipe is DeepSeek-R1 thinking prompt and trained on MATH level 3–5 data). On the 7B models, the performance are also very close to the RL results.
We then apply RL training with two different prompts (the Mathstral prompt and the DeepSeek-R1 thinking prompt), and 𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐛𝐨𝐭𝐡 𝐮𝐥𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐬𝐢𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐚𝐫 𝐬𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐬. As shown in Figures 2 and 3, training with the DeepSeek-R1 prompt initially improved rapidly due to fitting the format, and then its learning curve aligned with the Mathstral prompt.
My guess is that all the recent "weird" behaviors on Qwen models probably comes from continued pretraining on huge number of math QA pairs . For Qwen models, maybe you just find a suitable prompt by prompt optimization, and they can become reasoning machines.🤔

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Is LLM use finally making me less capable?
I started using LLMs three years ago for text and code gen. Now, I use several of them, for a ton more things.
In fact, I feel like I use them for a huge fraction of the cognitive tasks that I perform that can be described in text.
That is... an embarrassing large number of congitive tasks.
I've come to realize that all the cognitive offloading is making me feel less capable, not more. It used to be the case that early on, I felt like ChatGPT and Claude gave me super powers.
Now I sometimes feel like a slob, as my kneejerk reaction is to go and ask ChatGPT for help. It's always there, more than it used to be, and it's much better than it used to be, it will get much better than it currently is.
It's hard to measure tangibly how this cognitive performance differential, in terms of offloading, is manifested, but it feels like it's true to the point I'm convinced that there exists a law of "mental capacity" vs "offloading" that looks like this.
I'm sure someone is studying it already :)

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
🧵When training reasoning models, what's the best approach? SFT, Online RL, or perhaps Offline RL?
At @Krafton_AI and @SKtelecom, we've explored this critical question, uncovering interesting insights!
Let’s dive deeper, starting with the basics first.
1) SFT
SFT (aka hard distillation) is the very first approach you would try!
👍 This is very compute efficient as we don’t need to generate any responses from the model being trained.
👎 What are the downsides? We distill the behaviors only from the trajectories with correct answers (reward = 1). The model may learn the behaviors of generating correct answers, but not necessarily how to avoid writing incorrect reasonings. (Some believe that this is why RL generalizes better than SFT.)
2) Online RL
On the other hand, online RL works as follows. The model being trained first generates its own reasoning traces. The traces are graded, and the good traces get encouraged, and incorrect traces get discouraged. GRPO is an efficient reward renormalization method, and it is observed to make RL training converge better.
👎 What’s the downside? The cost of generating responses from the model being trained is huge! Every time you update the model, one needs to keep generating new responses using the new model parameter.
3) Offline RL
What’s something in between these two? Can we keep the efficiency of SFT while making use of negative examples too?
Offline RL strikes a balance between compute and learning efficiency. (In fact, SFT can be viewed as a special case of offline RL but only with positive reward samples!)
Offline RL is simple. It samples a batch of reasoning traces in the dataset and measures the rewards (which could be either positive or negative). That’s it 😁
No extra compute required for rollouts. It still accounts for negative examples as the reward gives you that signal.
4) Does offline RL work for training reasoning models?
The question is: Is this really useful? We don’t have definitive answers yet, but we have very interesting preliminary results.
We took the existing reasoning models (e.g., OpenThinker 2/3 for instance) and continued training them using offline GRPO.
The results were promising! With about 100 GPU hours, we were able to observe a marginal (a few percentage points) yet consistent reasoning accuracy improvement over diverse domains (AIME25, AMC23, LiveCodeBench, …)!
We found this pretty surprising for the following reasons:
1⃣ The amount of compute that went into this training procedure is less than 1% of the compute power that went into the preceding training process. The last-mile improvements on reasoning benchmark scores can be made with a single GPU node in a day 😊
2⃣ We only trained on the math dataset, but the model doesn’t seem to exhibit catastrophic forgetting on reasoning in other domains (if not slightly improved).
5) Technical challenges
There are a few technical details that we had to figure out to make this work.
1⃣ The existing reasoning traces dataset does not come with ground-truth answers for the questions. We used simple majority voting to find the pseudo-label for each question and defined the reward based on them, but a better method could be used to improve the quality of reward signals.
2⃣ Another technical challenge when it comes to offline-GRPO is the scenario where all the reasoning traces are correct. The vanilla offline GRPO cannot handle this, as after the reward normalization, all rewards become 0. This is fine for online RL (the generator is already good!), but it’s not good for offline cases. In fact, this happens about every six iterates while running GRPO! We came up with a very simple heuristic -- we added a positive bias term when this happens.
For more technical details, please refer to our technical blog:
We also released the continually trained offline-RL models:
6) What's next?
Lots of interesting questions remain open!
1⃣ What happens if we scale offline GRPO with more compute/data? We are working on it, so stay tuned for more updates!
In fact, together with @SKtelecom, at @Krafton_AI, we are building a strong R&D team dedicated to researching advanced LLM training algorithms and architectures, and this is one of our many research initiatives.
@Krafton_AI has a very strong group of researchers (see our recent work at
We are very pleased to team up with @SKtelecom, which has the leading expertise in LLM training and deployment with its long-standing efforts in open-source LLMs in Korea!
SKT has been making a significant contribution to LLMs for Korean researchers, from KoBERT, KoGPT, … to the recent release of A.X-3.1, an LLM trained entirely from scratch using their own stack! Check out their models at
2⃣ Also, what about if we use offline GRPO directly from pretrained models? Can we apply offline GRPO to the Qwen instruct models and possibly get a better reasoning model than OpenThinker? We should have a chat on this @AlexGDimakis @madiator :)
That's it for now! This preliminary report summarizes our early findings, intended to inform and engage the research community.
We're open to further discussion and collaboration, so please reach out with any feedback or interest!

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Excited about our new work:
Language models develop computational circuits that are reusable AND TRANSFER across tasks.
Over a year ago, I tested GPT-4 on 200 digit addition, and the model managed to do it (without CoT!). Someone from OpenAI even clarified they NEVER trained GPT-4 explicitly on 200-digit arithmetic. (can't find the tweet :( )
How?? It felt like magic. In controlled arithmetic tests on transformers, length generalization consistently failed. There must be something magic about pretraining?
Turns out there's a clean, simple, and plausible answer: Transfer.
Here is what we find with Jack @jackcai1206 Nayoung @nayoung_nylee, Avi @A_v_i__S, and my friend Samet @SametOymac:
Language models develop computational circuits that TRANSFER length generalization across related tasks.
A "main" task (like addition) trained on short sequences inherits length capabilities from an "auxiliary" task (like carry prediction) trained on longer sequences, if the model is co-trained on BOTH.
This happens even when we train from scratch on only task A and B. But it only happens when A and B are related.
So, length TRANSFERS between tasks, when they are similar. I think this is very cool!
We tested this across three types of tasks:
- arithmetic (reverse addition, carry operations)
- string manipulation (copying, case flipping)
- maze solving (DFS, shortest path).
Same pattern!
We also find that language pretraining acts as implicit auxiliary training. Finetuning checkpoints at different pretraining stages shows that more pretraining => better length generalization on downstream synthetic tasks.
After ~3 years studying length generalization, much of the initial magic has dissipated. And that's great! This is what science does. It lifts the veil of ignorance :)

summary:

2023-2024: Exploring arithmetic and length generalization in transformers, led by Kartik @KartikSreeni and Nayoung @nayoung_nylee.
2024-2025: Discovering transformers can learn arithmetic through self-generated data and self-improvement, work led by Nayoung @nayoung_nylee and Jack @jackcai1206.

Over a year ago, I tested GPT-4 on 200 digit addition, and the model managed to do it (without CoT!). Someone from OpenAI even clarified they NEVER trained GPT-4 explicitly on 200-digit arithmetic. (can't find the tweet :( )
How?? It felt like magic. In controlled arithmetic tests on transformers, length generalization consistently failed. There must be something magic about pretraining?
Turns out there's a clean, simple, and plausible answer: Transfer.
Here is what we find with Jack @jackcai1206 Nayoung @nayoung_nylee, Avi @A_v_i__S, and my friend Samet @SametOymac:
Language models develop computational circuits that TRANSFER length generalization across related tasks.
A "main" task (like addition) trained on short sequences inherits length capabilities from an "auxiliary" task (like carry prediction) trained on longer sequences, if the model is co-trained on BOTH.
This happens even when we train from scratch on only task A and B. But it only happens when A and B are related.
So, length TRANSFERS between tasks, when they are similar. I think this is very cool!
We tested this across three types of tasks:
- arithmetic (reverse addition, carry operations)
- string manipulation (copying, case flipping)
- maze solving (DFS, shortest path).
Same pattern!
We also find that language pretraining acts as implicit auxiliary training. Finetuning checkpoints at different pretraining stages shows that more pretraining => better length generalization on downstream synthetic tasks.
After ~3 years studying length generalization, much of the initial magic has dissipated. And that's great! This is what science does. It lifts the veil of ignorance :)

Why do small reasoners hallucinate??
High hallucination rate of facts, for smaller than 1T parameter reasoning models, like gpt-oss make sense to me.
These model have learnt HARD algorithms form training and RL on domain specific data that allow it to benchmaxx. These algorithms take up a lot of model capacity and will displace knowledge of facts.
It’s a battle between learning algorithms and memorizing tables.
But unlike the hardness of figuring out how to solve AIME or SWE, figuring out who Dimitris Papailiopoulos is, or retrieving any other discoverable fact on the web can be done with web search.
So perhaps it’s a matter of teaching these models one more skill, which is to know when you can’t recall facts and when one is requested you use a tool. And maybe that’s all that’s missing from small benchmaxxing reasoning models to mitigate hallucinations.

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Why is cross-entropy a good loss for language pretraining?
caveat: this is all known btw; interestingly, even though there are many viewpoints and intuitions on "why x-ent", they all can be arrived at from a single starting point.
Here's a simple first-principles derivation that doesn't assume anything about the data distribution. It comes from a very reasonable operational requirement :)
"I want my model to sound intelligent"
but we can't measure that, so we ask
"I want my model to sound like a human"
Although we have access to all texts ever written, we can't quite measure that either, so we instead ask
"I want my model to be as likely as possible to generate one of the texts ever written"
Or more bluntly:
"I want my model to memorize the training data."
Consider this thought experiment:
Given a dataset S of all text ever written by humans, we perform independent trials for each "text" in S:
Sample: "sample text" from our model Pr( ;W)
Check: did "sample text" exactly match the original? Note: we do not condition on anything! we just ask, of all the stuff the model could generate, did we get "text".
Define success as the event
E = "all per-sample checks succeed"
The probability of E is, the product of the probabilities assigned to the correct ground truth by your model W
Pr(E) = Π_{text in S} Pr(text; W)
Maximizing log Pr(E) over W gives you the cross-entropy objective.
How do you do you optimize this with SGD?
sample text from corpus
compute grad log Pr(token|prefix) for every prefix of text
update model
What's elegant is that this same simultaneously:
1) Minimizes the description length of the data under model P( ;W) (compression view)
2) Minimizes KL divergence to the true distribution—if one exists (though we never assumed one)
3) Implements maximum likelihood estimation
The derivation is straightforward and well-known, but it highlights something important:
cross-entropy emerges naturally from wanting exact reproduction of the training data.
P.S. you could have instead asked to maximize
Pr(text generated by the model is in ground truth)
interestingly, optimizing this can lead to mode collapse, since an optimal solution is to always predict a single piece of text from the corpus. Yet the gradients again look like x-entropy but with a multiplying factor
i.e., Pr(text;W) grad log Pr(text;W)

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Another interesting observation
performing SGD on x-entropy loss on your text corpus
is equivalent to
REINFORCE, i.e., on-policy policy gradient, with binary reward "Did my model generate text from corpus"

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Thinking Less at test-time requires Sampling More at training-time!
GFPO is a new, cool, and simple Policy Opt algorithm is coming to your RL Gym tonite, led by @VaishShrivas and our MSR group:
Group Filtered PO (GFPO) trades off training-time with test-time compute, in order to increase accuracy while decreasing the excess token length of reasoning caused by RL by up to ~80%.
It all comes down to creating "length pressure" to the model by sampling more attempts, and rejecting long ones, irrespective of correctness.
This leads the model to sounding much more laconic too, without sacrificing accuracy (in fact sometimes it's more accurate than the GRPO'd model)!
Detailed thread after the arxiv and github release!

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Sample More to Think Less: Group Filtered Policy Optimization for Concise Reasoning
"We introduce GFPO (Group Filtered Policy Optimization), which curbs this length explosion by sampling larger groups per problem during training and filtering responses to train on based on two key metrics: (1) response length and (2) token efficiency: reward per token ratio. By sampling more at training time, we teach models to think less at inference time. On the Phi-4-reasoning model, GFPO cuts GRPO's length inflation by 46-71% across challenging STEM and coding benchmarks (AIME 24/25, GPQA, Omni-MATH, LiveCodeBench) while maintaining accuracy. Optimizing for reward per token further increases reductions in length inflation to 71-85%. We also propose Adaptive Difficulty GFPO, which dynamically allocates more training resources to harder problems based on real-time difficulty estimates, improving the balance between computational efficiency and accuracy especially on difficult questions. GFPO demonstrates that increased training-time compute directly translates to reduced test-time compute--a simple yet effective trade-off for efficient reasoning."
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GyTzB1ubYAAxbog.jpg

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Origins story of GFPO (Sample More to Think Less):
Before the release of phi-4-reasoning, I was testing the model on HMMT using an internally hosted api call that supported up to 32k token generations.
I was dumb enough to not count gens>32k as failures, and so when a response would be partial (i.e., the model would not finish by 32k), I'd just reset and regenerate, till I got one within 32k.
We got the 32k numbers, they looked good, in fact, much much better than phi-4 without reasoning (40% gap)!! Then when the 64k api call was properly set up, I rerun the eval expecting that the performance would improve... and... the accuracy dropped!
What I was doing with the 32k call was rejection sampling, preferring short over long responses! This seemed to benefit accuracy over giving the model the chance to use up more tokens to complete a long attempt.
Interestingly, there were concurrent findings identical to this by @AlexGDimakis (he refers to it as Laconic Decoding) and @MichaelHassid. Both observed that shorter responses can be better, and there was a high correlation of long and bad.
It was clear at this point that this would very likely be reinforced, leading to models that are both accurate, and much more laconic and terse.
Ergo, GFPO.

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Imagine you're trying to teach a human how to do a task, say install Windows XP in a virtual machine. The human walks into a room and sees a document (prompt) that you have written, that describes exactly what they are supposed to do. There is also a computer ready for their keyboard inputs.
Then, they try for a while, and suppose they fail. Then, you write some detailed notes and new additional instructions in the prompt document, based on how they failed trying to teach them how to do the task.
But then, A NEW PERSON walks in and tries to solve the task. Every day, it's a fresh new employee and you can only update the document.
This Memento-like experience is how most companies are currently trying to train agents, by writing prompts (Multi-agent systems usually means multiple prompts) and is not going to lead to AGI.
But no wait, you should say, there is Reinforcement Learning post-training, this is the path to AGI, nicely summarized in the recent paper "The Era of Experience" by Silver and Sutton. With RL, the agent will try to solve the task and we will update their brain weights to increase the probability of good rollouts (successful attempts to install Windows) and decrease the probability of failed rollouts. This is good, but imagine trying to teach a human how to install Windows with this tormenting process: leaving them alone in a room, letting them bang their head into a wall and only when they manage to install Windows, update their brain weights a tiny bit. If they keep messing up, there will be no reward, no gradient and no learning. That is why agents must be post-trained with SFT first (basically observe other people solving the task end-to-end) and only after they can solve task 1 out of 10 times, RL can be deployed. You cannot talk to them during the process, you cannot give them verbal feedback on what error they made, they cannot think why they failed etc. One good signal that this process is sub-optimal is that RL trained agents keep getting GRPO gradients after re-solving the same math problem thousands of times, which shows that GRPO is extremely sample inefficient, compared to how humans learn.
Dwarkesh has a recent video "Why I don't think AGI is right around the corner".
He says that this lack of continual learning is showing that we lack a fundamental idea to reach human-level performance. He describes an example similar to mine but with teaching a kid to play the saxophone, while I set an arguably lower bar(?) of installing Windows.
Dwarkesh says "The reason humans are so useful is not mainly their raw intellect, its their ability to build up context, interrogate their own failures and to pick up small improvements as they practice a task."
I would summarize the challenge as follows: Right now, there is no established RL algorithm to give a model verbal feedback and have it update it's weights. There is also no established algorithm for a model to reflect on a previous failed execution and update it's own weights.
There are several methods (e.g. TextGrad, Reflexion, ALHF from Databricks and the now well-known GEPA) that update PROMPTS or create 'lessons learned' or memory summaries which are inserted into the prompt context, but this is still like a fresh new student walks in every day and things that cannot be explicitly verbalized cannot be learned.
On updating weights from feedback and reflection, there is significant on-going research e.g. I recently saw "Natural Language Reinforcement Learning (NLRL)" by Feng et al. and I'd love to get more pointers. I think that indeed we are entering the era of experience and we will need to find new algorithmic ideas before agents can learn as efficiently as humans.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GyXvIWha4AAYq7V.jpg

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Thinking about model generalization is quite painful.
We observe empirically that models trained with SGD on cross-entropy generalize, instead of just memorize the train data. Even when they have sufficient capacity to memorize.
We do not---i repeat--- we. do. not. have a mathematical proof for why this happens. Don't let anyone convince you otherwise :D
A common current hypothesis involves the 'implicit bias' of SGD, i.e., that gradient descent somehow favors "simple" or "generalizing" solutions. That sounds pleasing, because it's plausible, but we can't precisely define what "simple" means in a manner that is precise. We also can't quite prove why this "bias" leads to the generalization we observe.
This is very deep open problem in machine learning.
Why does SGD find generalizing solutions when memorizing solutions also exist?
The fact that our models become SIMULATORS rather than MEMORIZERS isn't explained by the loss function, algorithm, model arch, data alone.
It emerges from the INTERACTION between the loss function, the optimization algorithm, the model architecture, and the structure of language itself.
We do not understand this, it's an empirical gift that SGD on cross entropy against a model trained on human data produces simulators...
P.S. Please don't just share the arxiv link to your paper that explains generalization :)

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Language models should be trained to create their own tools!
Language models can use tools, but they can't create their own tools at a complexity level similar to humans.
What are tools? Tools are computational shortcuts for patterns you see repeatedly, or for tasks that just take too much of an effort to do yourself.
That is largely not how language models operate today!
LLMs solve similar problems from scratch every time. They don't recognize patterns across interactions. They don't discover and don't build shortcuts. Every interaction starts effectively fresh, even when there's memory features like in the ChatGPT app.
This is kinda strange. A model might solve a gazillion similar math/code problems, each time using its full capacity. It does not discover this pattern. Most certainly it does not abstract it into a reusable artifact, i.e., a tool.
The tools btw don't have to be code snippets. There can and likely should be far more complex than that. They could be predictive models themselves, learned functions (why not language models??). Anything that takes a pattern the model keeps encountering and turns it into something reusable *is* a tool.
Why is this currently hard? Many reason I suppose, but the main three are "discovery", "verification", and I guess.. "they models are not trained to do it".
How does a model figure out it's doing something repeatedly when there's no permanence between interactions? The model needs to see through a very large scale and across its own reasoning traces and user interactions to discover repetition. Sounds hard!
Also, how do you know that 1) a tool works and 2) it works better than doing things yourself? Again, hard to imagine without long-horizon play, feedback, a huge sandbox to play in. Also how do you do this without being explicitly trained for this?
And so who cares and does this matter? I think it does, because a model that creates tools can improve after deployment!!
Current models are static, after you train and deploy, the capabilities are frozen. A "tool creator" becomes more effective, perhaps more capable as interactions scale. An effective tool creator effectively optimize itself with the discovery of new tools. This is a form of "self improvement" that happens without changing the weights of the model itself (but maybe that's also important).
I suppose it's cool to think of a world where models act as their own tool makers. Going beyond the tools that we give them (calculators/interpeters/other frozen models etc). Creating their own computational shortcuts, their own models of prediction, based on what they discover across millions of tokens of interactions.
My speculation is that this (no tool creation) is part of whatever we think is "the wall".

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Congrats to @jackcai1206 and @nayoung_nylee for their NeurIPS Spotlight on "Extrapolation by Association: Length Generalization Transfer In Transformers" :)
Quoting @DimitrisPapail
Excited about our new work:
Language models develop computational circuits that are reusable AND TRANSFER across tasks.
Over a year ago, I tested GPT-4 on 200 digit addition, and the model managed to do it (without CoT!). Someone from OpenAI even clarified they NEVER trained GPT-4 explicitly on 200-digit arithmetic. (can't find the tweet :( )
How?? It felt like magic. In controlled arithmetic tests on transformers, length generalization consistently failed. There must be something magic about pretraining?
Turns out there's a clean, simple, and plausible answer: Transfer.
Here is what we find with Jack @jackcai1206 Nayoung @nayoung_nylee, Avi @A_v_i__S, and my friend Samet @SametOymac:
Language models develop computational circuits that TRANSFER length generalization across related tasks.
A "main" task (like addition) trained on short sequences inherits length capabilities from an "auxiliary" task (like carry prediction) trained on longer sequences, if the model is co-trained on BOTH.
This happens even when we train from scratch on only task A and B. But it only happens when A and B are related.
So, length TRANSFERS between tasks, when they are similar. I think this is very cool!
We tested this across three types of tasks:
- arithmetic (reverse addition, carry operations)
- string manipulation (copying, case flipping)
- maze solving (DFS, shortest path).
Same pattern!
We also find that language pretraining acts as implicit auxiliary training. Finetuning checkpoints at different pretraining stages shows that more pretraining => better length generalization on downstream synthetic tasks.
After ~3 years studying length generalization, much of the initial magic has dissipated. And that's great! This is what science does. It lifts the veil of ignorance :)

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Small models as the new frontier and why this may be academia's LLM moment
Academia should reject the nihilism of "scale is all you need", i.e, that meaningful research requires frontier scale compute. This mindset hurts basic research and what we can contribute to machine learning in practice.
Many interesting questions about architectures, data, and training methods do show signal and can be tested at the O(100M) to O(1B) parameter scale within reasonable budget. There seems to exist no fundamental reason why these insights wouldn't transfer and hold up to 14B, 32B, or even larger models. Yes, there will be trends and observations that break at the trillion parameter scale, but my conjecture is that this will be irrelevant for the majority of models people will actually deploy locally in the future.
The economics of post-training (SFT/RL) are finally favorable for academia. Post training a 7B model fits on a single H100 GPU, which roughly $3/hour on cloud providers. You can train on 100M+ tokens for under $100.
Why care about mid/post-training? That's where a lot of interesting problems are! Reasoning, tool use, specialization, etc, these are settings where you see meaningful performance improvements and skills learnt within millions of trained tokens, not billions, that are typical for pretraining.
More importantly, the 4B-32B parameter range will likely dominate local deployment in the not so distant future. These models fit on reasonable hardware (a beefy laptop) as inference requires enough RAM to fit the model, but you can use without GPUs for single batch inf calls. Also these models, at that scale, are getting seriously good for tasks likecoding, math, tutoring, computer use etc.
So here is my conjecture: local models at the <100B scale will eventually generate more tokens/day than api-hosted frontier models.
This may be academia's moment! The open-weights ecosystem provides a path to real impact without million-dollar GPU clusters at this scale.
Our research can directly study, understand, and improve the 99% of models that will run locally, not the 1% that require data centers. This is finally both possible and meaningful. Don't be discouraged by scale maximalism!!

Here’s a scaling law that matters more: every two years the gap to frontier closes by a factor of 2x
Quoting @karpathy
Excited to release new repo: nanochat!
(it's among the most unhinged I've written).
Unlike my earlier similar repo nanoGPT which only covered pretraining, nanochat is a minimal, from scratch, full-stack training/inference pipeline of a simple ChatGPT clone in a single, dependency-minimal codebase. You boot up a cloud GPU box, run a single script and in as little as 4 hours later you can talk to your own LLM in a ChatGPT-like web UI.
It weighs ~8,000 lines of imo quite clean code to:
- Train the tokenizer using a new Rust implementation
- Pretrain a Transformer LLM on FineWeb, evaluate CORE score across a number of metrics
- Midtrain on user-assistant conversations from SmolTalk, multiple choice questions, tool use.
- SFT, evaluate the chat model on world knowledge multiple choice (ARC-E/C, MMLU), math (GSM8K), code (HumanEval)
- RL the model optionally on GSM8K with "GRPO"
- Efficient inference the model in an Engine with KV cache, simple prefill/decode, tool use (Python interpreter in a lightweight sandbox), talk to it over CLI or ChatGPT-like WebUI.
- Write a single markdown report card, summarizing and gamifying the whole thing.
Even for as low as ~$100 in cost (~4 hours on an 8XH100 node), you can train a little ChatGPT clone that you can kind of talk to, and which can write stories/poems, answer simple questions. About ~12 hours surpasses GPT-2 CORE metric. As you further scale up towards ~$1000 (~41.6 hours of training), it quickly becomes a lot more coherent and can solve simple math/code problems and take multiple choice tests. E.g. a depth 30 model trained for 24 hours (this is about equal to FLOPs of GPT-3 Small 125M and 1/1000th of GPT-3) gets into 40s on MMLU and 70s on ARC-Easy, 20s on GSM8K, etc.
My goal is to get the full "strong baseline" stack into one cohesive, minimal, readable, hackable, maximally forkable repo. nanochat will be the capstone project of LLM101n (which is still being developed). I think it also has potential to grow into a research harness, or a benchmark, similar to nanoGPT before it. It is by no means finished, tuned or optimized (actually I think there's likely quite a bit of low-hanging fruit), but I think it's at a place where the overall skeleton is ok enough that it can go up on GitHub where all the parts of it can be improved.
Link to repo and a detailed walkthrough of the nanochat speedrun is in the reply.

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Not All Bits Are Equal: What We Learned From 1700 Experiments on Memory-Optimal Reasoning
Given a fixed memory budget, how should you allocate across model weights, KV cache, and test-time compute to maximize accuracy in reasoning models?
For example: would you choose a 32B, 4-bit model with a 14k token budget, or an 8B, 16-bit model with 30k tokens?
We ran 1,700 experiments on the Qwen3 family to find out. We varied:
- Model size (0.6B-32B),
- Weight precision (4/8/16-bit via GPTQ),
- Serial test-time compute (token budgets 2k→30k via budget forcing),
- Parallel test-time compute (Maj@K, up to K=16),
- KV cache compression (eviction: R-KV, StreamingLLM; quantization: HQQ at 2/4/8-bit).
This is great work led by my Krafton/UW collaborators @jhyuckkim (Krafton), @ethan_ewer (undergrad!! at UW-Madison), @taehong_moon (Krafton), @jon_ghoh (UC Berkeley)
Here is a summary of the main findings:
At the 4B+8-bit threshold optimal mem strategy flips
For models effectively smaller than 8-bit 4B, spend memory on more (or higher-precision) weights, not on longer generations. For larger models, do the opposite: allocate memory to longer generations until performance saturates.
This threshold isn't arbitrary, i.e., it is right at the point where weights dominate KV cache/token count.
The reasoning task matters (eg your mileage may vary, no universal recipe!)
Math reasoning (eg AIME25): 4-bit quantization is almost always a bad idea. An 8B model at 16-bit outperforms a 14B model at 4-bit with similar memory spent. The numerical precision in weights seems to matter for "reasoning heavy" tasks. Almost as if the model’s capacity to utilize test time compute is decimated by quantization...
Knowledge heavier tasks (GPQA-D): 4-bit is broadly memory-optimal. Here, parameter count matters more than precision. The interpretation is that here you want more effective weights to store things, and raw parameter count dominates test time compute.
How does parallel test time compute (fancy for majority voting) factor in?
Majority voting (Maj@K) increases KV cache linearly with K. It improves the mem–acc trade-off only when the model is >= 8-bit 4B effective size; the optimal K grows with the memory budget. Below that scale, serial test time compute should be preferred.
Weight quantization alone isn't enough!
Both KV cache eviction and KV quantization push the mem optimal Pareto frontier higher across all model sizes we tested.
Should you prefer KV evict or quant?
- Small models (<8-bit 4B): KV cache eviction wins
- Large models (≥8-bit 4B): Both strategies competitive
Latency/throughput note:
End-to-end latency is dominated by generation length. When you care a lot about latency, 8-bit often sits at a better speed–accuracy point than 4-bit.
Note on batching:
When model weights, i.e., params, are amortized across concurrent generations (that is, batched inference), the tradeoff shifts, as you’d expected. At a batch size of 16 the 0.6B model never appears on the Pareto. The 4B-8bit model always appears no matter the batchsize in the ~1-2GB memory region (good model setting for mobile devices!)
What This Means
***There is no universal memory-optimal strategy for reasoning models!***
The right choice depends on almost every parameter involved, but here is one way to choose:
If effective size < 8-bit 4B
--- Spend your bits on model capacity/precision over longer token budgets.
--- Prefer 8-bit for math-heavy tasks.
--- Use KV eviction over KV quantization.
--- Stick to serial scaling; Maj@K is memory-inefficient here.
If effective size ≥ 8-bit 4B
---Increase token budget till gains saturate.
---Maj@K always helps, so grow K with available memory.
---KV quantization is competitive with eviction; choose based on implementation and maybe taste 😊
Important Caveat: These findings are specific to the Qwen3 family on AIME25 and GPQA-D. The thresholds and strategies will vary with different architectures, training methods, and task distributions.

This is great work led by my Krafton/UW collaborators @jhyuckkim (Krafton), @ethan_ewer (undergrad!! at UW-Madison), @taehong_moon (Krafton), @jon_ghoh (UC Berkeley)
Here is a summary of the main findings:
At the 4B+8-bit threshold optimal mem strategy flips
For models effectively smaller than 8-bit 4B, spend memory on more (or higher-precision) weights, not on longer generations. For larger models, do the opposite: allocate memory to longer generations until performance saturates.
This threshold isn't arbitrary, i.e., it is right at the point where weights dominate KV cache/token count.
The reasoning task matters (eg your mileage may vary, no universal recipe!)
Math reasoning (eg AIME25): 4-bit quantization is almost always a bad idea. An 8B model at 16-bit outperforms a 14B model at 4-bit with similar memory spent. The numerical precision in weights seems to matter for "reasoning heavy" tasks. Almost as if the model’s capacity to utilize test time compute is decimated by quantization...
Knowledge heavier tasks (GPQA-D): 4-bit is broadly memory-optimal. Here, parameter count matters more than precision. The interpretation is that here you want more effective weights to store things, and raw parameter count dominates test time compute.
How does parallel test time compute (fancy for majority voting) factor in?
Majority voting (Maj@K) increases KV cache linearly with K. It improves the mem–acc trade-off only when the model is >= 8-bit 4B effective size; the optimal K grows with the memory budget. Below that scale, serial test time compute should be preferred.
Weight quantization alone isn't enough!
Both KV cache eviction and KV quantization push the mem optimal Pareto frontier higher across all model sizes we tested.
Should you prefer KV evict or quant?
- Small models (<8-bit 4B): KV cache eviction wins
- Large models (≥8-bit 4B): Both strategies competitive
Latency/throughput note:
End-to-end latency is dominated by generation length. When you care a lot about latency, 8-bit often sits at a better speed–accuracy point than 4-bit.
Note on batching:
When model weights, i.e., params, are amortized across concurrent generations (that is, batched inference), the tradeoff shifts, as you’d expected. At a batch size of 16 the 0.6B model never appears on the Pareto. The 4B-8bit model always appears no matter the batchsize in the ~1-2GB memory region (good model setting for mobile devices!)
What This Means
***There is no universal memory-optimal strategy for reasoning models!***
The right choice depends on almost every parameter involved, but here is one way to choose:
If effective size < 8-bit 4B
--- Spend your bits on model capacity/precision over longer token budgets.
--- Prefer 8-bit for math-heavy tasks.
--- Use KV eviction over KV quantization.
--- Stick to serial scaling; Maj@K is memory-inefficient here.
If effective size ≥ 8-bit 4B
---Increase token budget till gains saturate.
---Maj@K always helps, so grow K with available memory.
---KV quantization is competitive with eviction; choose based on implementation and maybe taste 😊
Important Caveat: These findings are specific to the Qwen3 family on AIME25 and GPQA-D. The thresholds and strategies will vary with different architectures, training methods, and task distributions.

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Not All Beans Are Equal: What I've Learned From 1700 Experiments on Taste-Optimal Coffee Bean Roasting
Quoting @DimitrisPapail
it depends what you're comparing against. Here are some facts:
- roasting is relatively quick: a batch of 160g (typically 8-10 coffee cups) takes <15 minutes to prepare (though you need to let it rest for 1-2 days).
- the overall cost per lb of home roasting is much lower than store bought beans: a 1LB bag of the highest end green beans typically costs less than 10$. The cost of 1lb of roasted, high-end beans is 40-70$.
- roasting very good tasting at light/medium levels is relatively easy after a few tries. The learning curve is not steep at all. I'd even say brewing with a v60 has around the same or more tuning knobs than roasting actual beans.
- brewing an average home roast is an unfathomable number of times better tasting than an average coffee shop's drip.
Your question however was whether the final cup enjoyment is higher. My speculative answer to that is that if on top of the above you're also a person that enjoyes to cook/prep meals for yourself/others, then I'd be surprised if you didn't love roasting your own beans.
Overall the effort involved is low, the cost much less than a high end roasting company, and it is legitimately a lot of fun experimenting with.

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Diffusion Language Models' Last Exam
very cool !
Quoting @Kangwook_Lee
DLLMs seem promising... but parallel generation is not always possible
Diffusion-based LLMs can generate many tokens at different positions at once, while most autoregressive LLMs generate tokens one by one.
This makes diffusion-based LLMs highly attractive when we need fast generation with less compute.
A big question is … is parallel generation possible without losing modeling accuracy?
The answer is no. There are fundamental limits on how much parallelism we can achieve.
Consider this example:
“Pick one city uniformly at random from the following four cities:
New York, New Orleans, Mexico City, or Panama City.”
Then,
P(Y₁ = New, Y₂ = York) = 1/4,
P(Y₁ = New, Y₂ = Orleans) = 1/4, and so on.
Thus, P(Y₁ = New) = 1/2, P(Y₂ = City) = 1/2.
If you choose to generate Y₁ and Y₂ in parallel, no matter which decoding algorithm you use …
You’re doomed to sample “New City.”
None of today’s DLLMs can generate these two words correctly without giving up parallelism.
-----
Why is this the case?
In fact, we never train LLMs to learn the joint distribution over multiple tokens in one forward iteration.
We always teach a single-token marginal distribution conditioned on context.
(The same holds for autoregressive models too.)
Therefore, sampling multiple tokens at once is only possible when those tokens are mutually independent given the current context.
And this limitation of parallel sampling can be precisely formalized.
One can derive an information-theoretic limit that’s decoding-strategy agnostic, and also derive strategy-specific limits.
-----
So are DLLMs doomed? No!
They have huge potential to save compute and time.
But:
(1) we need to be aware of their fundamental limitations, and
(2) we need to design better training and decoding strategies.
In particular, there’s huge room for improvement in decoding.
Why?
Ideally, we want the model to control the degree of parallelism during generation.
At the same time, it should choose a subset of future tokens that are almost mutually independent given the current context.
Are current decoding strategies good at this?
Hard to tell.
Most DLLMs were never stress-tested for it.
-----
That’s why we introduced a synthetic benchmark to stress-test DLLMs.
We call it ParallelBench.
The idea is simple: these are natural language tasks, but carefully designed so that parallel generation is inherently difficult.
(Think “New City”, but more natural, real tasks.)
What did we find?
We tested popular DLLMs with various decoding algorithms, and none came close to “oracle” performance, the ideal performance you’d get if the model could optimally adjust its parallelism during decoding.
-----
Takeaway:
(1) Parallel generation is not always possible and check out our paper for more details :)
(2) If you can design a DLLM that matches oracle performance on our benchmark, well, who knows, you might just get a call from someone in Menlo Park. 😉

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
DeepSeek-OCR is cool but not that cool.
Quoting @Kangwook_Lee
A more serious thread on the DeepSeek-OCR hype / serious misinterpretation going on.
1.
On token reduction via representing text in images, researchers from Cambridge have previously shown that 500x prompt token compression is possible (ACL'25, Li, Su, and Collier).
Without using the idea of converting text to images.
2.
We shouldn't attribute the success of DeepSeek OCR to the power of image representation.
At the same time, there's nothing fundamentally wrong with text representation with whatever tokenizer.
In fact, you can do the opposite of what DeepSeek-OCR did, i.e., you can represent images as a sequence of text tokens (each representing their RGB values), and things will just work fine. (See the LIFT paper.)
3.
The only correct takeaway is that the current embedding spaces used by LLMs are just enormous and maybe even very wasteful.
And importantly, we’re not making full use of them yet.
4.
There is much recent evidence supporting the same message.
For instance, it is shown that if you provide in context demonstrations from multiple tasks but mixed in a single context, then your model can solve multiple ICL prediction tasks simultaneously. (See the EVERYTHING EVERYWHERE ALL AT ONCE paper.)
5.
tldr;
- DeepSeek-OCR is cool
- but you can achieve a higher token reduction rate by just finetuning LLMs on squeezed text tokens
- there is more evidence that LLMs are not fully utilizing the large embedding space and the huge amount of compute that goes in at inference time
- and that's the only real take away you should take away

summary:
unbelievable
Quoting @natolambert
I'm convinced to try it asap, we should all try fp16, look at this plot man. FP16 is like perfect in error reduction.
"This is precisely why switching to FP16 provides a fundamental solution. With its 10 mantissa bits, FP16 offers 8 times more precision (2^10 values vs. 2^7 values) than BF16. This higher fidelity means that the outputs of the training and inference engines are much more likely to be numerically identical. The increased precision creates a buffer that absorbs the minor implementation differences between the two engines, preventing rounding errors from accumulating and causing a policy divergence.
For RL fine-tuning, the dynamic range of the model’s weights and activations has already been established during pre-training. Therefore, the extreme range of BF16 is less critical, while the precision it sacrifices becomes a dominant drawback. By reverting to FP16, we trade the unnecessary range of BF16 for the critical precision, effectively closing the gap between training and inference without any complex algorithmic or engineering workaround."

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Are you using LLM-as-a-judge? Yeah you're using it wrong. Here's why and how to fix it.
Quoting @Kangwook_Lee
LLM as a judge has become a dominant way to evaluate how good a model is at solving a task, since it works without a test set and handles cases where answers are not unique.
But despite how widely this is used, almost all reported results are highly biased.
Excited to share our preprint on how to properly use LLM as a judge.
🧵
===
So how do people actually use LLM as a judge?
Most people just use the LLM as an evaluator and report the empirical probability that the LLM says the answer looks correct.
When the LLM is perfect, this works fine and gives an unbiased estimator.
If the LLM is not perfect, this breaks.
Consider a case where the LLM evaluates correctly 80 percent of the time.
More specifically, if the answer is correct, the LLM says "this looks correct" with 80 percent probability, and the same 80 percent applies when the answer is actually incorrect.
In this situation, you should not report the empirical probability, because it is biased. Why?
Let the true probability of the tested model being correct be p.
Then the empirical probability that the LLM says "correct" (= q) is
q = 0.8p + 0.2(1 - p) = 0.2 + 0.6p
So the unbiased estimate should be
(q - 0.2) / 0.6
Things get even more interesting if the error pattern is asymmetric or if you do not know these error rates a priori.
===
So what does this mean?
First, follow the suggested guideline in our preprint.
There is no free lunch. You cannot evaluate how good your model is unless your LLM as a judge is known to be perfect at judging it.
Depending on how close it is to a perfect evaluator, you need a sufficient size of test set (= calibration set) to estimate the evaluator’s error rates, and then you must correct for them.
Second, very unfortunately, many findings we have seen in papers over the past few years need to be revisited.
Unless two papers used the exact same LLM as a judge, comparing results across them could have produced false claims. The improvement could simply come from changing the evaluation pipeline slightly. A rigorous meta study is urgently needed.
===
tldr:
(1) Almost all LLM-as-a-judge evaluations in the past few years were reported with a biased estimator.
(2) It is easy to fix, so wait for our full preprint.
(3) Many LLM-as-a-judge results should be taken with grains of salt.
Full preprint coming in a few days, so stay tuned!

Quoting @DimitrisPapail
Not All Bits Are Equal: What We Learned From 1700 Experiments on Memory-Optimal Reasoning
Given a fixed memory budget, how should you allocate across model weights, KV cache, and test-time compute to maximize accuracy in reasoning models?
For example: would you choose a 32B, 4-bit model with a 14k token budget, or an 8B, 16-bit model with 30k tokens?
We ran 1,700 experiments on the Qwen3 family to find out. We varied:
- Model size (0.6B-32B),
- Weight precision (4/8/16-bit via GPTQ),
- Serial test-time compute (token budgets 2k→30k via budget forcing),
- Parallel test-time compute (Maj@K, up to K=16),
- KV cache compression (eviction: R-KV, StreamingLLM; quantization: HQQ at 2/4/8-bit).
This is great work led by my Krafton/UW collaborators @jhyuckkim (Krafton), @ethan_ewer (undergrad!! at UW-Madison), @taehong_moon (Krafton), @jon_ghoh (UC Berkeley)
Here is a summary of the main findings:
At the 4B+8-bit threshold optimal mem strategy flips
For models effectively smaller than 8-bit 4B, spend memory on more (or higher-precision) weights, not on longer generations. For larger models, do the opposite: allocate memory to longer generations until performance saturates.
This threshold isn't arbitrary, i.e., it is right at the point where weights dominate KV cache/token count.
The reasoning task matters (eg your mileage may vary, no universal recipe!)
Math reasoning (eg AIME25): 4-bit quantization is almost always a bad idea. An 8B model at 16-bit outperforms a 14B model at 4-bit with similar memory spent. The numerical precision in weights seems to matter for "reasoning heavy" tasks. Almost as if the model’s capacity to utilize test time compute is decimated by quantization...
Knowledge heavier tasks (GPQA-D): 4-bit is broadly memory-optimal. Here, parameter count matters more than precision. The interpretation is that here you want more effective weights to store things, and raw parameter count dominates test time compute.
How does parallel test time compute (fancy for majority voting) factor in?
Majority voting (Maj@K) increases KV cache linearly with K. It improves the mem–acc trade-off only when the model is >= 8-bit 4B effective size; the optimal K grows with the memory budget. Below that scale, serial test time compute should be preferred.
Weight quantization alone isn't enough!
Both KV cache eviction and KV quantization push the mem optimal Pareto frontier higher across all model sizes we tested.
Should you prefer KV evict or quant?
- Small models (<8-bit 4B): KV cache eviction wins
- Large models (≥8-bit 4B): Both strategies competitive
Latency/throughput note:
End-to-end latency is dominated by generation length. When you care a lot about latency, 8-bit often sits at a better speed–accuracy point than 4-bit.
Note on batching:
When model weights, i.e., params, are amortized across concurrent generations (that is, batched inference), the tradeoff shifts, as you’d expected. At a batch size of 16 the 0.6B model never appears on the Pareto. The 4B-8bit model always appears no matter the batchsize in the ~1-2GB memory region (good model setting for mobile devices!)
What This Means
***There is no universal memory-optimal strategy for reasoning models!***
The right choice depends on almost every parameter involved, but here is one way to choose:
If effective size < 8-bit 4B
--- Spend your bits on model capacity/precision over longer token budgets.
--- Prefer 8-bit for math-heavy tasks.
--- Use KV eviction over KV quantization.
--- Stick to serial scaling; Maj@K is memory-inefficient here.
If effective size ≥ 8-bit 4B
---Increase token budget till gains saturate.
---Maj@K always helps, so grow K with available memory.
---KV quantization is competitive with eviction; choose based on implementation and maybe taste 😊
Important Caveat: These findings are specific to the Qwen3 family on AIME25 and GPQA-D. The thresholds and strategies will vary with different architectures, training methods, and task distributions.

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Reasoning models are special, and each one follows its own odd CoT path. ReJump, from @yzeng58, gives a super clean way to visualize that reasoning path. It takes a raw CoTs and turns them into a tree, where the jumps are Calculate/Verify/Backtrack. This allows you to actually see how a model reasons, loops over steps, branches and explores.
It's cool to use it and visualize how different models look once you map them this way. They can have the same acc on a task, but totally different style: some explore wide, others go deep, some verify a lot (cough.. phi-4-r), others never check their work and kind of zero shot their solution. We of course knew all this anecdotally, but now there’s a more systematic way to measure it.
ReJump is actually useful: it allows you to both visualize reasoning and offers a common language to analyze how models solve problems. you can measure overthinking, under- or over-verification, wasted backtracking, and improve Best of N, and I'd argue even the way we train these models with RL.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7u18xUWcAAJI2o.jpg
Quoting @Kangwook_Lee
[ReJump: How Reasoning LLMs Actually Think]
Modern LLMs can solve really challenging problems, as they not only just generate answers right away given the question, but instead go through a long form, step by step thought process, or so called "reasoning".
Since the debut of OpenAI's o1, and then a surprising rise of DeepSeek's R1, lots of research has been focusing on what it means and how to make LLMs reason better.
As a result, we have a variety of LLMs that achieve really high accuracy on solving challenging tasks, such as solving math problems, programming tasks, etc.
But what about the actual reasoning process behind the final accuracy numbers?
If two models achieve the same level of accuracy on challenging tasks, do they actually go through similar reasoning processes?
Or can it be the case that two models achieve the same level of accuracy but have completely different reasoning styles?
Surprisingly, we still do not have a good tool to answer this question.
In our new preprint, led by my students and collaborators from UW Madison (@UWMadison), Microsoft Research (@MSFTResearch), FuriosaAI (@FuriosaAI), SNU (@SeoulNatlUni), and KRAFTON (@Krafton_AI), we propose ReJump, one of the very first solutions to this problem.
Our idea is simple. Given an LLM, we first run inferences on a reasoning task. Every reasoning trace is just a bunch of natural language sentences, that is, a linear representation of the reasoning process.
We then reconstruct a hidden tree representation of the reasoning trace. The tree representation is very useful. We can represent an intermediate derivation or thought as a node, and the root node as the prompt.
We can represent the derivation outcome of a parent node as its child node, and branches as multiple ideas to try out given the previous state, etc.
With this definition, we can effectively represent intermediate states (or thoughts in the chain of thought) as nodes of a tree and represent their relationships as edges.
We then reconstruct a “jump” process. Similar to the standard graph or tree walk process, it is a sequence of nodes, but the next move does not need to be to adjacent nodes, so we call it a tree “jump”.
(How do we actually reconstruct the tree and jump process? We developed an LLM agent that is specialized in parsing the trace and reconstructing the underlying tree and jump process. See the paper for more details.)
In sum, we map a linear reasoning trace into a tree representation and a jump process on it, and we call this representation ReJump.
===
So what can we do with ReJump?
1) In depth understanding and comparison of LLMs’ reasoning behaviors
Well, first of all, we finally can better understand LLMs’ reasoning behaviors beyond the accuracy. We can measure how large reasoning trees are, how deep they are, how widely they jump around on a tree (local vs global exploration), how frequently they revisit states they visited before without realizing it (that is, forgetting), or how frequently they intentionally revisit the states they visited before for the purpose of verification, etc.
You can also compare two reasoning traces more systematically by comparing the structural similarities between the trees or similarities between the temporal patterns of the jump processes.
Here is an example. DeepSeek-R1, Phi-4, and Claude 3.7 Sonnet can all get this simple math puzzle instance correctly.
However, if you visualize the ReJump representation of their generated reasoning traces, you can see that there are a whole lot of different things going on behind the scenes.
R1 notably attempts lots of different ideas and explores widely, and it takes a lot of time for it to figure out the right path.
On the other hand, both Phi-4 and Claude 3.7 Sonnet get the answer without much exploration.
(This is a very interesting phenomenon as itself, and it probably means that a model could think deeply in the latent space to evaluate the potential of an idea instead of spitting it out of its mouth in the form of token generation.)
This is just one example, but you could do this at a dataset level and get more interesting insights about how different reasoning models behave.
For instance, you can compare many reasoning models and evaluate many different properties of their ReJump representations to get insights as shown above.
What I found most interesting is the comparison of models before and after RL training on reasoning tasks.
From these charts above, you can easily tell what RL training provides models with. To my eyes, the most notable thing is that they seem to have learned how to explore!
2) More than just understanding?
We present several useful applications of ReJump beyond just understanding and comparing LLMs’ reasoning.
a) Better analysis of in context reasoning examples.
Since LLMs are good at in context learning, we can actually equip a non reasoning LLM with a few reasoning traces generated by a teacher model and expect it to behave like a reasoning model.
From the accuracy standpoint, the accuracy seems to go up, but are we really sure they are actually implementing similar reasoning algorithms?
From our preliminary experiments, it seems like they do. Here, we are using R1 traces as in context reasoning examples and providing them to Gemini 2.0 Flash and DeepSeek V3.
As we provide an increasing number of examples, they not only improve their accuracies, but their generated trees and jumps become closer and closer to those from the teacher model.
b) Better understanding of which emergent properties contribute the most to successful reasoning.
Instead of just staring at the reward during RL training, we can actually see the ReJump analysis during RL training.
To show the usefulness of this approach, we RL trained Qwen3-1.7B on a simple math puzzle task (Game of 24).
During RL training (the x axis here is the number of training steps), we see a huge uptick both in accuracy and verification rate.
A more thorough investigation needs to be done, but there are lots of exciting applications of ReJump in better understanding what happens during RL training for reasoning.
c) ReJump based Best of N and prompt tuning.
You can also use the ReJump representation to come up with your BoN strategy or tune your prompts.
Let us say you computed the ReJump statistics on your validation set and found a high correlation between the answer being correct and a particular ReJump metric, say jump distance.
By knowing this, you can implement a jump distance based BoN, that is, generate N responses and pick the one whose jump distance is the highest.
Similarly, you can even add this as a part of the prompt (either natural language instruction or in context reasoning examples with large jump distances).
We show both approaches work.
===
So what’s next?
It has been a little over a year that we as a whole research community have been collectively working on how to make LLMs reason better.
Mostly we have been focusing on how to train them using various algorithms, hoping to improve their accuracy.
However, there are millions of ways of getting the same answer, and we have seen related ideas like Laconic Decoding in the past.
By going further, ReJump looks into reasoning traces and tries to fully understand how reasoning traces are structured.
Lots of open problems. The current ReJump agent is very costly, so that is one thing. Another thing is to directly incorporate ReJump analysis as part of reward or model training and see if it helps.
===
This project took a lot of time and effort from my students and collaborators, and I want to give special kudos to my former student Yuchen Zeng (@yzeng58) and collaborators Shuibai (@ShuibaiZ69721) and Wonjun. Thanks as well to the senior authors who jointly advised the whole team with me, my best collaborator Dimitris (@DimitrisPapail) and Hyung Il.
===

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Still trying to understand the relative value of harness/scaffold vs raw model capabilities for agent tasks, e.g., TerminalBench. There's an interesting attribution question.
For example: In TerminalBench, there's a ~10% gap between Opus 4.5 in Claude Code vs Droid (another scaffold), and a ~10% gap between Opus 4.5 and Sonnet 4.5 within Claude Code. Both feel significant.
What's odd about harnesses is that "test-time compute" becomes hard to normalize, as there are different number of api calls and orchestration logic (eg involving scratchpad/tools etc.)
There's a few good questions i am super curious about:
- As models improve, do scaffold gains shrink?
- if 10% gains can come from either a better model or a better scaffold, what should we optimize?

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
Every once in a while a new use case emerges with chat models for me. The newest: going on long walks and recording very long voice messages describing projects, current or future ideas, social situations that need some analyzing etc.
This has led to heavily using voice-to-text and dramatically increasing the number of input tokens to the model.
I find that voice lets me capture way more nuance because I can keep on going at whatever pace feels natural to me. Text doesn't allow this as much, even though I type reasonably fast.
There's also something about walking, as it increases focus when explaining things in a way that sitting at a computer doesn't and kinda allows me to go into very long length unstructured info dumps. That part feels significant.
In some weird way the model is much better and appears much more capable when I do this. I think it's because voice increases my personal "context window capacity" eg I'm able to add much more nuance by just babbling a lot about a topic (cough old prof habits never go away) that the models are actually very capable of grasping.
It's been pretty cool! Has allowed me to use these models much more as a collaborator rather than an autocomplete and has increased the capacity of my communication channel to them.
Try it!

title: Dimitris Papailiopoulos (@DimitrisPapail)
summary:
What's the tradeoff between (Model Size, Quantization, Test-time Compute, Accuracy)?
Come to ICLR to find out how we interpret 1700 experiments attempting to address this question :)
Quoting @DimitrisPapail
Not All Bits Are Equal: What We Learned From 1700 Experiments on Memory-Optimal Reasoning
Given a fixed memory budget, how should you allocate across model weights, KV cache, and test-time compute to maximize accuracy in reasoning models?
For example: would you choose a 32B, 4-bit model with a 14k token budget, or an 8B, 16-bit model with 30k tokens?
We ran 1,700 experiments on the Qwen3 family to find out. We varied:
- Model size (0.6B-32B),
- Weight precision (4/8/16-bit via GPTQ),
- Serial test-time compute (token budgets 2k→30k via budget forcing),
- Parallel test-time compute (Maj@K, up to K=16),
- KV cache compression (eviction: R-KV, StreamingLLM; quantization: HQQ at 2/4/8-bit).
This is great work led by my Krafton/UW collaborators @jhyuckkim (Krafton), @ethan_ewer (undergrad!! at UW-Madison), @taehong_moon (Krafton), @jon_ghoh (UC Berkeley)
Here is a summary of the main findings:
At the 4B+8-bit threshold optimal mem strategy flips
For models effectively smaller than 8-bit 4B, spend memory on more (or higher-precision) weights, not on longer generations. For larger models, do the opposite: allocate memory to longer generations until performance saturates.
This threshold isn't arbitrary, i.e., it is right at the point where weights dominate KV cache/token count.
The reasoning task matters (eg your mileage may vary, no universal recipe!)
Math reasoning (eg AIME25): 4-bit quantization is almost always a bad idea. An 8B model at 16-bit outperforms a 14B model at 4-bit with similar memory spent. The numerical precision in weights seems to matter for "reasoning heavy" tasks. Almost as if the model’s capacity to utilize test time compute is decimated by quantization...
Knowledge heavier tasks (GPQA-D): 4-bit is broadly memory-optimal. Here, parameter count matters more than precision. The interpretation is that here you want more effective weights to store things, and raw parameter count dominates test time compute.
How does parallel test time compute (fancy for majority voting) factor in?
Majority voting (Maj@K) increases KV cache linearly with K. It improves the mem–acc trade-off only when the model is >= 8-bit 4B effective size; the optimal K grows with the memory budget. Below that scale, serial test time compute should be preferred.
Weight quantization alone isn't enough!
Both KV cache eviction and KV quantization push the mem optimal Pareto frontier higher across all model sizes we tested.
Should you prefer KV evict or quant?
- Small models (<8-bit 4B): KV cache eviction wins
- Large models (≥8-bit 4B): Both strategies competitive
Latency/throughput note:
End-to-end latency is dominated by generation length. When you care a lot about latency, 8-bit often sits at a better speed–accuracy point than 4-bit.
Note on batching:
When model weights, i.e., params, are amortized across concurrent generations (that is, batched inference), the tradeoff shifts, as you’d expected. At a batch size of 16 the 0.6B model never appears on the Pareto. The 4B-8bit model always appears no matter the batchsize in the ~1-2GB memory region (good model setting for mobile devices!)
What This Means
***There is no universal memory-optimal strategy for reasoning models!***
The right choice depends on almost every parameter involved, but here is one way to choose:
If effective size < 8-bit 4B
--- Spend your bits on model capacity/precision over longer token budgets.
--- Prefer 8-bit for math-heavy tasks.
--- Use KV eviction over KV quantization.
--- Stick to serial scaling; Maj@K is memory-inefficient here.
If effective size ≥ 8-bit 4B
---Increase token budget till gains saturate.
---Maj@K always helps, so grow K with available memory.
---KV quantization is competitive with eviction; choose based on implementation and maybe taste 😊
Important Caveat: These findings are specific to the Qwen3 family on AIME25 and GPQA-D. The thresholds and strategies will vary with different architectures, training methods, and task distributions.
